# **Cassie Zawilski’s Agenda Doc** {#cassie-zawilski’s-agenda-doc}

Cassie, moderator of JSC 249, created a VERY good agenda [doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_qmxKiJBk57_tiAiT8C98AgptcEcoSRcMmZpSUvEF6I/edit?usp=sharing). 

We highly recommend you review it and [use](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_qmxKiJBk57_tiAiT8C98AgptcEcoSRcMmZpSUvEF6I/edit?usp=sharing) it (make a copy of it and rename it for your JSC).

The official *Never Search Alone* agenda doc above is an overview. 

Cassie’s is more detailed and we recommend you consider using it (and if you do, send her an email to thank her – cassandra.zawilski@gmail.com).

# **Three-Part Meeting Structure**

Here is the three-part structure for a 2 hour meeting:

| Agenda Item | Details | Suggested Length |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Updates & Homework Reflection | Share updates with one another, including any individual homework (as proposed in the first 10 agendas above) |  30 \- 60 (depending on homework or exercise) |
| Short RFHs (requests-for-help) | During member updates, see if there are RFHs that can be addressed or solved in just a couple minutes, triage those first. |  \~ 30 minutes |
| Long RFHs and Joint Exercises | Longer RFH conversations, as well as any joint exercises from the book \- again refer to the First 10 Agendas tool to center your theme for the meeting |  \~ 30 \- 60 minutes |

Your first official meeting is important to setting the rhythm for your ongoing meetings. 

After you get going and you have built trust and close bonds, then feel free to decide as a JSC to make changes to the format I recommend.

Before I say more about the three-part meeting structure, let me first say a few words about building trust.

### 

### Video \- How to Build Trust {#video---how-to-build-trust}

As a moderator, your most important job is to build trust on your JSC.

And your first question will likely be: “How do I do that?”

First, watch this [video](https://vimeo.com/868380339/71d9031f0d?share=copy) of JSC moderators talking about how they have built trust.

There are lots of good details in there.

The good news is that trust is relatively easy to build on JSCs because of several intentional decisions about the environment and norms that we emphasize.

1. Asking-for-help environment.  
   Most importantly, in your charter and in everything you do, you should constantly and consistently emphasize your JSC as a place to ask for help. 

   As I outline in Chapters 1 and 2 in *Never Search Alone*, asking for help is the key concept at the heart of a good job search \*and\* if you emphasize asking for help in recruiting JSC members it will naturally “compel the humble and repel the arrogant.”

   This is important because humility is key to asking for help and building trust.

2. Cognitive empathy and the power of strangers  
   Trust also gets built via “cognitive empathy” – a concept I explain in Chapter 1 of the book. Cognitive empathy simply means you are with others going through a similar experience. Further, cognitive empathy seems to be strengthened when you are paired with strangers or acquaintances, rather than close friends or colleagues. Re-read Chapter 1 for more on this important concept.

3. Commitment to attend and participate  
   In your charter, I ask you each to commit to a cadence of meetings, to confidentiality, and to really attending and being there for each other. This also goes a long way towards building trust.

Finally, I ask you and each of your members to give trust to gain trust. What I mean by that is I encourage you to ask your members to be open and vulnerable – share their insecurities and anxieties and discover 1\) that they are not alone; and 2\) that by coming together they will help deepen the trust environment on your JSC.  
   
Note: see again Cassie’s detailed [agenda](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_qmxKiJBk57_tiAiT8C98AgptcEcoSRcMmZpSUvEF6I/edit?usp=sharing) doc for how to run your meeting zero, which is your trust-building session.

### 

### Example Meeting (2 hours) {#example-meeting-(2-hours)}

**5 minutes early (-00:05)**

Set a norm that everyone strives to arrive 5 minutes early so that people can settle, say hello informally, and be prepared to begin on time

**Start of meeting/update prep (00:00 – 00:05)**

Review the agenda for this meeting, including any homework or exercises. Send the update forms (see appendix of this doc for a good JSC update form).

**Part 1: Updates & Homework reflection (00:05 – 0:35)**

Begin updates. Every member gets 5 minutes. Assign one member to be the timekeeper with their smartphone (set a 4-minute alarm so they can inform the speaking member when they have 1 minute left)

Moderator takes confidential notes during the updates listening for possible short and long RFHs.

**Part 2: Short RFHs \- requests for help (00:35 \- 01:00)**

Short RFH is a 15 – 30-minute discussion on a more tactical question (i.e. question about the listening tour, candidate-market fit, interviewing, negotiating, etc.)

**Part 3: Long RFHs** 

You can do 1-2 long RFHs in the last 90 minutes or so of your meeting

These are the difficult/challenging questions that members may have in their job search.

    
**The three challenges of asking for help**  
Below I outline some of the challenges you and your fellow members may have in asking for help. These are especially important for your moderator to understand.

1\. Member does not actually know the question they want to ask  
The member may be struggling with the question itself. In this case, the role of the JSC is first to non-judgmentally clarify the question. The non-judgmental part is important. We all have moments when we do not quite know the question we want to ask but know that we need help. It is important to cultivate every attempt by your fellow members to ask for help \- especially if they are unsure what they are asking for. \[examples and short case studies will be provided\]  
   
2\. Member knows the question, knows the course of action but cannot act  
This is very common. Often members will have a sense of the problem and “know” what to do but cannot act. In cases like these, members will often not ask for help because they think they know the answer – and they likely do. But because in life as in behavioral economics “knowing” the answer is often not enough, it’s important to establish and reinforce with your members that this is exactly the kind of question/situation they should bring to the JSC.   
   
3\. Member knows the question, thinks they know the answer, but has a blind spot  
This is similar to above but with a twist. In this case, it’s not that they know what to do but can’t act, it’s that they think they know but are missing something. Perhaps your fellow member cannot see how they are entertaining an offer from a company that does not fit their Mnookin Two-Pager. Maybe they are driven by anxiety to take the first thing that comes along. Maybe they have been reluctant to negotiate for budget, resources, and support – or maybe they are skipping the Listening Tour. 

This is where the JSC can make a big difference as long as there’s trust built in the room so that members are open to hearing a different perspective or having their blind spots challenged.   
   
**The three challenges of responding to a member’s question**  
1\. You or your fellow members do not understand the question  
Perhaps your requesting member was unclear or maybe they spoke using jargon or lingo. It’s very important that you and your fellow members understand the question. So ask clarifying questions. Read the room. Are people engaged? Disconnected? Confused? Don’t move on until everyone understands.  
   
2\. The question is clear and the problem is clear but it’s hard to talk about  
The second challenge that often comes up is the challenge of giving a member hard-to-deliver feedback. It is hard to challenge a bias or blind spot of a fellow member. Many people will shy away from being so direct. First, the member asking has to be clear that they want direct feedback. That is important. As moderator, you might need to check in with them several times to confirm and reconfirm that. Second, if you sense members are having a hard time, then encourage them to couch their response in language like this: “This is hard to say and it’s possible that I’m wrong but if you’ll allow me let me share with you what I see that you may not be able to see…”  
   
3\. The member can’t (or won’t) hear what you are saying  
Perhaps the requesting member has said they want direct feedback, and perhaps your members have given them feedback. Yet, the requesting member keeps twisting the feedback to fit into their existing paradigm or blind spot. If members around the JSC start to pick up on this, then it has to be directly addressed. You need to check in with the requesting member and give them direct feedback that they seem not open at this moment to what their fellow members are saying to them. Ask them if they are aware of that dynamic. Ask your fellow members to comment on it. You may want to suggest perhaps that the JSC return to this issue in a month or two. Whatever you do, it has to be done non-judgmentally and in the spirit that we all have blind spots and difficulties getting those blind spots challenged.   
   
**The three challenges of hearing feedback from fellow members**  
   
1\. People want confirmation they are right  
No matter who we are – or how much experience we have with managing confirmation bias – we all want confirmation we are right. This can be exacerbated by the confidence hit we might have taken in the events leading up to a job search. The JSC is designed to directly contradict this when necessary (obviously there are many times when a member’s decision or course of action seems right). It is hard to hear feedback that you missed something, that you are seeing it in a distorted way, or perhaps asking the wrong question. As moderator, you should as much as possible model yourself by hearing feedback that challenges your own confirmation bias. And you should be patient with your fellow members’ struggle with this.  
   
2\. People often don’t really want to make any changes  
This is related to point 1 but it’s often true that we are more comfortable – sadly – with ways of working that don’t work. If a JSC points out some blind spot or bias, it might challenge the way we see ourselves. For example, lots of research confirms that people with insecurity often hang on to it because it’s a known and long-patterned way of being. Again, you should model willingness to change and be patient with your fellow members.  
   
3\. Sometimes the JSC gets it wrong – or the member disagrees  
Just because others can see our biases when we can’t does not necessarily mean that others are necessarily ‘right.’ As moderator, your role should be to make sure members truly hear what is being said. Then make clear it’s up to the member what they want to do. Always, you should maintain a spirit of non-judgment in the JSC.   
   
The good news is that if you recruited the right people and follow the structure I’ve outlined above – and use the templates that I make freely available – then the odds are good that your JSC will work and members will help each other. You can make mistakes as a moderator. Your members can be conflicted about asking for real help and hearing the feedback. Yet, everyone will still get a lot of value. In my experience, leaders are desperate for environments like these and even a little bit of help goes a long way.   
   
Having said that, here are some additional important moderator practices that will help you succeed.  
 

### **Moderator best practices** {#moderator-best-practices}

   
1\. Listen  
Moderators and members must listen. I’ve developed a simple framework that I call 3 audience listening. You have three audiences you need to listen to when moderating a JSC: 1\) the member speaking at the moment; 2)the JSC as a whole; 3)yourself. Each of these are important.   
   
2\. Keep the trains running on time  
Certainly for your first several meetings, one of your key roles is to start and end the meetings, and each section of the meetings, on time. If a good conversation is happening, you can allow a few minutes of leeway. Otherwise, you need to jump in and cut off dialogue and move forward.   
   
3\. Enforce the rules  
You need to enforce the rules of your JSC as outlined in your charter and agreed to by members. To some this sounds petty, but being on time and being present at each JSC meeting is critical to creating trust. If members start to come late or not at all, it will destroy your JSC. You need strong accountability and a shared sense of commitment to create the trust for everyone to participate in the activity of asking for help. Please also remember that rules and norms can be revisited \- what worked at the formation of a JSC might not still fit as the council evolves.  
   
4\. Model asking for help and being vulnerable  
One of your important jobs is to model asking for help and hearing the feedback as I discussed in more detail above. That means you have to show something you don’t know –and the more vulnerable or risky the better.   
 

# **What if Your JSC Goes Off-Track?** {#what-if-your-jsc-goes-off-track?}

What should you do if your JSC is not bonding? If members are not really opening up? Or not showing up consistently?

First and foremost, reach out to the moderator team (as moderator you’ll be on a Slack channel with other moderators) and ask for help.

Secondly, below I outline some common problems

**1\. No one is taking risks or really asking for help** 

If no one is taking risks or asking for help, then first you need to model that behavior yourself. In my long experience, it only takes one person opening up and asking for help to create enough trust for more people to follow. So, again, you should be that first person. Don’t ask a tactical question – ask one that you think doesn’t make you look good (ironically, that is NOT how your fellow members will think of you – it’s just how you fear they will think of you). For example, let’s say you are a chief product officer looking for your next job and let’s say a company made a verbal offer and then withdrew it. Talk about that. Be open. Be vulnerable. Ask your JSC for help navigating this. First, they will be relieved to discover that you are an imperfect human in imperfect environments like everyone else. Second, you will be relieved to discover that your problem is not that unusual. 

**2\. People are asking for help but ignoring or twisting the feedback**

The single event that will bond your JSC is when a member asks for help and the JSC responds and has an impact. On the other hand, if your members are asking for help but then not allowing the feedback of the JSC to have an impact, then everyone gets demoralized. What if you are following my directions above and going through the process I’ve outlined for making sure questions are good and answers are clear and feedback is received? What if, despite that, members are still twisting or ignoring the feedback? Well then it just confirms you are all humans. This is very common especially early on in a JSC. It’s so common that I have a name for it. I call it Croesus’ Curse. 

Croesus was the rich king of Lydia, an ancient empire that was one of the first to coin money. He was the richest person in the world at that time and he was interested in conquering the neighboring Persian Empire. To advise him on this decision, Croesus carefully asked for help – first by testing which Oracle was truly reliable, and then having identified the best Oracle, he asked what would happen if he invaded Persia. The Oracle responded that a great empire would fall. 

The first problem here is \- true to the ways of Oracles \- was that the answer was vague. Whose kingdom?  

Croesus, however, did not probe further. Instead, he assumed the Oracle meant the Persian Empire would fall if he invaded. 

Generally speaking, when you have a JSC where people are asking for help but it’s not having an impact, then I would assume two things are going on at the same time: the responses from members are like the Oracle’s – i.e. too vague, and the requester is like Croesus twisting the responses to fit a bias. Both dynamics usually operate at the same time. 

If that’s the case, then you have fallen prey to Croesus’ Curse. Croesus took the Oracle’s vague advice, fit it into his own plans, and invaded Persia. Sadly, the Persians fought back and overthrew Croesus and the Lydian Empire. In the end a great empire did fall – but it was Croesus who lost his crown not Cyrus, the King of Persia. 

In fact, Croesus is one of the first recorded instances of asking for help in human history – and of Croesus’ Curse in acting on that help. 

Every JSC will struggle with Croesus’ Curse. 

You should talk about it in advance, expect it to come up, and then ignore it when it does first surface. That’s right – ignore it. Just make note of it as a moderator and keep going. It’s fine if it happens at first. In fact, expect it. If you try to battle it right away, then people will get demoralized. The good news is that job seekers are so desperate for safe environments like a JSC that even a little bit of help goes a long way. What you want, instead, to look for is the first instance where someone really asks for help and really hears what the members have to say. You should help make that happen but remember it takes time.

If, after 3 meetings or more, you have not been able to create at least one instance where a member asks for help and gets feedback that changes how they are searching, then talk with your JSC. Explain what you have seen and ask for their input on how to make the experience more valuable for everyone. 

Building a safe zone where you and your fellow members can ask for help and challenge yourselves is powerful, simple, but also hard – it’s emotionally challenging. And this is even more true for successful leaders who have accomplished a lot. It’s hard for them (and you) to be open about challenges. 

Be patient. Make sure all your members come to every meeting. Come on time. Turn devices off (except Zoom of course, if you are on Zoom). 

Be 100% present. Follow the process outlined above. 

Most of the time you will eventually bond and one day you’ll discover there’s a lot of trust, that members are truly asking for help and that you are having a real impact on each other’s search. 

 

# **Appendix: Update Form**

Here’s a sample update form you can ask your JSC members to fill out at each meeting.

1. Emotional pulse  
   On a scale of zero to 10 \-- how is your emotional balance been this week? Be honest. 

   And why did you give that score above?  
     
2. Homework  
   If we had homework, did you complete it…? Please briefly share what you did.

3. Do you need any help with any aspect of your search?  
   Please share whatever you need help with and we’ll try to address it in either a short RFH or long RFH session today.
